item.title: 2009: Yankees Beat Phillies 7-3, Win 27th World Series Title
item.description: The New York Yankees beat the Philadelphia Phillies 7–3 in Game 6 of the World Series, to clinch their 27th World Championship title, the most in all of sports. Yankees DH Hideki Matsui, who gains Most Valuable Player honors, drives in six runs, tying the record set by Bobby Richardson (1960 WS) and Will Clark (1989 NLCS) for most runs batted in a postseason game, while Andy Pettitte, pitching on three days' rest… Photo: edogisgod (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2021: Buster Posey Retires After 12 Seasons With Giants
item.description: Buster Posey announces his retirement after 12 seasons with the San Francisco Giants and winning three World Series championships with the team in 2010, 2012 and 2014. He was also the 2020 comeback player of the year. Photo: Ian D'Andrea (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2021: Posey Joins Elite Group of Lifetime Giants Players
item.description: Posey announced his retirement from baseball on November 4, 2021, making him just the fifth player in the San Francisco era to spend his entire career with the Giants (minimum of 10 seasons), joining Jim Davenport (1958–1970), Scott Garrelts (1982–1991), Robby Thompson (1986–1996) and former battery mate Matt Cain (2005–2017). Photo: Ian D'Andrea (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2017: SoftBank Hawks Beat BayStars 4-2, Win 2017 Japan Series
item.description: The Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks win the 2017 Japan Series for their fourth series title in seven years, topping the Yokohama DeNA BayStars 4 games to 2. Dennis Sarfate, who saved two wins and pitched three innings for the victory, was named the Series MVP. It is the first time American players have won back-to-back Japan Series MVP honors, as Brandon Laird did it in 2016. Photo: Gaffky (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2016: Doerr Becomes Oldest Living Former Major Leaguer
item.description: On November 4, 2016, Doerr became the oldest living former major leaguer upon the death of Eddie Carnett. Photo: Unknown author (Public domain).

item.title: 2014: Terry Francona Signs Two-Year Extension With Indians
item.description: Terry Francona and the Cleveland Indians agree to a two-year extension through 2018 with club options for both the 2019 and 2020 seasons. Francona's previous four-year contract with the Indians ran through the 2016 season, but the Indians will now have as many as four additional years of control should they choose. Photo: Keith Allison on Flickr (CC BY-SA 2.0).

item.title: 2014: Twins Hire Molitor as Manager, Introduce Him at Press Conference
item.description: The Twins hired Molitor to fill their manager vacancy for the 2015 season, and introduced him in a press conference on November 4, 2014. Photo: Paul Morse (Public domain).

item.title: 2013: Canadians Named 2013 Recipient of John H
item.description: On November 4, 2013, the Canadians were named the 2013 recipient of the John H.

item.title: 2012: Moehler Hired as Georgia Area Scout for Red Sox
item.description: On November 4, 2012, Moehler was hired as a Georgia area scout for the Boston Red Sox. Photo: SBoyd (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2010: Sparky Anderson, 76, Hall of Fame Manager
item.description: Sparky Anderson, 76, Hall of Fame manager; first manager to win the World Series in both leagues with the Cincinnati Reds (1975–1976) and Detroit Tigers (1984); in his playing days, a second baseman who played one MLB season for the 1959 Philadelphia Phillies. Photo: grgbrwn (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 2009: Yankees Win 7-3 in Game 6, Clinch World Series
item.description: With the series-clinching 7–3 New York victory in Game 6 on November 4, 2009, Yankee Stadium also became the latest stadium to host a World Series-clinching victory by its home team in the venue's first season (after the St. Photo: Adc95 (CC BY-SA 4.0).

item.title: 2002: Hinske Named AL Rookie of the Year, Jennings NL
item.description: It was a busy rookie awards day. First Eric Hinske of the Toronto Blue Jays was named American League Rookie of the Year getting 19 of the 28 first-place votes while the National League Rookie of the Year was won by Colorado Rockies' Jason Jennings who himself got 27 of the 32 first-place votes. Photo: Wknight94 (CC BY-SA 3.0).

item.title: 2001: Diamondbacks Beat Yankees 3-2, Win First World Series
item.description: The Arizona Diamondbacks win the first World Series of their four-year existence with a come-from-behind 3–2 win over the New York Yankees. Mariano Rivera, considered by many to be the best closer in postseason history, begins the bottom of the 9th inning with a 1-run lead, but is unable to protect it, allowing two runs, including a game-winning RBI single by Luis González.

item.title: 1994: Gooden Suspended for 1995 Season After Cocaine Test
item.description: Free agent pitcher Dwight Gooden is suspended for the entire 1995 season after testing positive for cocaine while already serving a 60-day suspension for a previous positive cocaine test. Photo: slgckgc (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1988: Nolan Ryan, Mike Schmidt Headline 1988 Free-Agent Class
item.description: The free-agent "Class of 1988" is joined by 75 players granted the opportunity under the terms of the CBA to test the market for their services. Two future Hall of Famers headline the class: Nolan Ryan and Mike Schmidt. Photo: Chuck Andersen Delaywaves (CC BY 2.0).

item.title: 1987: Benito Santiago Unanimous NL Rookie of the Year
item.description: One day after McGwire's triumph, San Diego Padres catcher Benito Santiago becomes the National League's Rookie of the Year by unanimous vote. He's the fourth consensus NL ROTY since 1956, and the first since Vince Coleman (1985).

item.title: 1982: Ferraro, 38, Appointed Manager of Cleveland Indians
item.description: Mike Ferraro is appointed manager of the 1983 Cleveland Indians. Former MLB infielder and minor-league skipper Ferraro, 38, has been a New York Yankees' coach since 1979.

item.title: 1980: Sadaharu Oh Retires With 868 Career Home Runs
item.description: Sadaharu Oh announces his retirement as a player from Japanese baseball. His 868 documented career home runs remains an unapproached world record among professional baseball players. Photo: ウィキ太郎(Wiki Taro) (Public domain).

item.title: 1963: Mets Trade Roger Craig to Cardinals for Two Players
item.description: The New York Mets trade pitcher Roger Craig to the St. Louis Cardinals for young pitcher Bill Wakefield and veteran outfielder George Altman. Craig, 33, went 15–46 (including an 18-game personal losing streak) for the expansion Mets but he will help the Cardinals win the 1964 World Series.

item.title: 1961: Kid Mohler, 90, Naval Academy Head Baseball Coach
item.description: Kid Mohler, 90, whose playing career lasted 24 seasons spanning 1890 to 1914 but appeared in only three games in majors as a rare, left-handed-throwing second baseman for Washington of the National League in 1894; head baseball coach, U.S. Naval Academy, 1929 to 1932; member, Pacific Coast League Hall of Fame.

item.title: 1959: Ernie Banks Wins Second Straight NL MVP Award
item.description: Ernie Banks of the Chicago Cubs wins the National League Most Valuable Player Award for the second straight year with 232 points. Eddie Mathews (189) and Hank Aaron (174) of the Milwaukee Braves finish second and third respectively. Photo: Pro's Pizza (Public domain).

item.title: 1955: Cy Young, 88, Hall of Fame Pitcher, 511 Wins
item.description: Cy Young, 88, Hall of Fame pitcher who won a record 511 games over a 22-year career with five clubs from 1890 to 1911, being a 30-game winner five seasons, a 20-game victor sixteen times, pitching a perfect game, two no-hitters, and while being a member of the 1903 Boston Americans hurling the first pitch in a World Series game. Photo: Bain News Service (Public domain).

item.title: 1953: Athletics Replace Dykes With Player-Manager Joost, 37
item.description: In what some see as a cost-cutting measure, the Philadelphia Athletics replace skipper Jimmy Dykes with player-manager Eddie Joost, 37, the club's longtime shortstop. Photo: Bain News Service, publisher (Public domain).

item.title: 1950: Grover Cleveland Alexander, 63, Hall of Fame Pitcher
item.description: Grover Cleveland Alexander, 63, Hall of Fame pitcher who played for the Philadelphia Phillies, Chicago Cubs and St. Louis Cardinals over 20 seasons (1911 through 1930), winning three pitchers' triple crowns (1915–1916; 1920) and setting a modern record for a rookie with 28 wins (1911), while collecting three seasons with 30-plus wins and leading the National League in wins (six times), strikeouts (six), earned run… Photo: Charles M. Conlon (Public domain).

item.title: 1949: Larry Douglas, Pitcher for 1915 Baltimore Terrapins
item.description: Larry Douglas, pitcher who played in 1915 for the Baltimore Terrapins of the outlaw Federal League. Photo: Wikimedia Commons (Public domain).

item.title: 1947: Browns Drop Ruel After Last-Place 59-95 Season
item.description: Muddy Ruel is dropped as manager of the St. Louis Browns after one season at the helm. His team finished last in the American League at 59–95 in 1947. Former Browns coach and interim manager James "Zack" Taylor, 49, will take his place. Photo: Bain News Service, publisher (Public domain).

item.title: 1941: Dolph Camilli Wins NL MVP in Landslide Vote
item.description: Dolph Camilli, hard-hitting Brooklyn Dodgers first baseman, is the BBWAA's landslide choice as Most Valuable Player in the National League for 1941. With 19 of 24 first-place votes and 300 points, he surpasses teammate Pete Reiser's three votes and 183 points.

item.title: 1904: Charlie Reilley, 47, Catcher for Troy Trojans, Reds
item.description: Charlie Reilley, 47 [?], catcher who hit .210 from 1879 through 1884 for the Troy Trojans, Cincinnati Reds, Detroit Wolverines, Worcester Ruby Legs and Boston Reds.

item.title: 1889: Brotherhood Issues Manifesto Decrying Players as Sheep
item.description: The Brotherhood of Professional Base-Ball Players issues its Manifesto stating that "players have been bought‚ sold and exchanged as though they were sheep instead of American citizens."

item.title: 1884: Mullane Signs With Cincinnati Red Stockings for 1885
item.description: Tony Mullane signs a contract with the Cincinnati Red Stockings for the 1885 season, in direct conflict with his prior oral agreement to play for the St. Louis Browns. The American Association will suspend Mullane for the entire 1885 season because of this and previous contract troubles, but allow him to remain the property of Cincinnati. Photo: Goodwin & Company (Public domain).
